Serampore
ser'êm-pôr
n. (Serampore, a Danish settlement on the Hooghly above Calcutta; the mission station of Carey, Marshman and Ward from 1800)
Bengali Shrirampur, the town of Sri Rama; Danish Frederiksnagore.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Serampore was a small Danish colony fifteen miles above Calcutta, and the three Baptist missionaries settled there in 1800 because the East India Company would not permit missionary work in its own territory. William Carey, Joshua Marshman and William Ward formed what became known as the Serampore Trio and lived under a common agreement: pooled income, shared household, a monthly reading of their covenant, and a mission run as a family. In thirty-four years they translated the Scriptures in whole or part into about forty languages and dialects, set up a printing press and a paper mill, founded Serampore College in 1818 to train Indian ministers in their own tongues, campaigned against sati and infanticide, and published the first Bengali newspaper. Isa 55:11 is the promise under the press. Psa 68:11 describes what came off it. Mat 28:19 is the commission the Company tried to exclude.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a press as a machine for printing; and translation, as the act of turning into another language; version.

expand to see more

PRESS, n. An instrument or machine by which any body is squeezed; a machine for printing; called a printing press.

TRANSLA'TION, n. The act of turning into another language; interpretation; a version.

COL'LEGE, n. A society of persons engaged in common pursuits; an edifice appropriated to the use of students.

Key Scripture

Isa 55:11 — "So shall my word be that goeth forth out of my mouth: it shall not return unto me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please, and it shall prosper in the thing whereto I sent it."

Psa 68:11 — "The Lord gave the word: great was the company of those that published it."

Mat 28:19 — "Go ye therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost:"

1Co 3:6 — "I have planted, Apollos watered; but God gave the increase."

Modern Corruption

Three men under one roof translated Scripture into forty tongues on a press they built themselves.

expand to see more

The Serampore agreement is the part most worth imitating and least imitated. The three read it aloud together three times a year, and it bound them to set no value on money except as it advanced the kingdom, to live simply, to esteem one another, and to keep the Indian people constantly in view as the mission's object rather than its background. Ecc 4 and 1Co 3:6 both bear on it: distinct labours, one increase from God, and no competition between the labourers.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. It does rebuke two things. First, the separation of translation from church planting, as though the text could be delivered and the congregation left to someone else; Serampore did both. Second, the assumption that commercial interests and missions are natural allies. The East India Company excluded missionaries for decades because conversion was bad for trade, and Isa 55:11 is the answer to that calculation, since the word accomplishes what God pleases regardless of what a company prefers.

Usage

"“it shall prosper in the thing whereto I sent it” (Isa 55:11) — forty translations."

"“great was the company of those that published it” (Psa 68:11) — off a mission press."

"“I have planted, Apollos watered” (1Co 3:6) — three men, one increase."
